[1;38;5;208mSTAGE 4 — Commands, streams, composition[0m

Three lessons, then a gate. You'll read a command's structure, check
whether a command exists, and chain commands together with pipes,
redirects, and globs.

Commands this stage:
  [1;38;5;220mcommand -v[0m   ask the shell if a program is installed
  [1;38;5;220mwc[0m           word, line, and character count
  [1;38;5;220mseq[0m           generate number sequences
  [1;38;5;220mhead[0m          first N lines of input
  [1;38;5;220msort[0m          sort lines
  [1;38;5;220mgrep[0m          select lines matching a pattern
  [1;38;5;220m|[0m             [1;38;5;244mpipe[0m: send one command's output into the next
  [1;38;5;220m>[0m             [1;38;5;244mredirect[0m: write output to a file (overwrites)
  [1;38;5;220m>>[0m            [1;38;5;244mappend[0m: add output to the end of a file
  [1;38;5;220m<[0m             [1;38;5;244minput redirect[0m: read a file into a command
  [1;38;5;220m*[0m

[1;38;5;244mglob[0m: match many filenames at once

[1;38;5;208m▶ Type [1;38;5;220mnext[1;38;5;208m to begin lesson 4.1.[0m

[1;38;5;208m4.1 — reading a command[0m

A shell command has a small grammar:

  [1;38;5;244mcommand  options  arguments[0m

Examples:
  [1;38;5;220mls[0m
  [1;38;5;220mls -l[0m                    [2m# one option, no argument[0m
  [1;38;5;220mls -l /etc[0m               [2m# option + argument[0m
  [1;38;5;220mwc -l poem.txt[0m           [2m# count lines in a file[0m
  [1;38;5;220mecho "hello world"[0m       [2m# argument with a space — quoted[0m

[1;38;5;196mSpaces matter.[0m  The shell splits on spaces. If a filename
has a space, [1;38;5;244mquote it[0m or the shell will see two arguments:

  [1;38;5;220mvim "my notes.txt"[0m       [2m# opens one file[0m
  [1;38;5;220mvim my notes.txt[0m         [2m# opens TWO files: 'my' and 'notes.txt'[0m

[1;38;5;244mcommand -v[0m asks the shell whether a command exists.
  [1;38;5;220mcommand -v ls[0m            [2m# prints the path; exits 0[0m
  [1;38;5;220mcommand -v vim[0m           [2m# does Vim exist

on this system?[0m
  [1;38;5;220mcommand -v vimtutor[0m      [2m# does vimtutor?[0m

[1;38;5;208m▶ Try a few [1;38;5;220mcommand -v[1;38;5;208m probes, then [1;38;5;220mnext[1;38;5;208m.[0m

-rw-r--r--@ 1 verlyn13  staff  141 Nov  7 16:54 numbers.txt
-rw-r--r--@ 1 verlyn13  staff  147 Nov  7 16:54 poem.txt

[1;38;5;208m4.2 — the pipe[0m

A [1;38;5;244mpipe[0m ( [1;38;5;220m|[0m ) sends the standard output of one
command into the standard input of the next. [1;38;5;196mMost important idea
in the shell.[0m

[1;38;5;220mwc[0m alone counts:
  [1;38;5;220mwc -l poem.txt[0m          [2m# lines in poem.txt[0m

[1;38;5;220mwc[0m via pipe counts [1;38;5;244mwhatever you piped in[0m:
  [1;38;5;220mseq 1 100 | wc -l[0m       [2m# 100[0m
  [1;38;5;220mls /usr/bin | wc -l[0m     [2m# how many programs are installed[0m

Pipes stack:
  [1;38;5;220mls /usr/bin | sort | head[0m        [2m# list → sort → first 10[0m
  [1;38;5;220mls /usr/bin | grep ^a[0m            [2m# names starting with 'a'[0m
  [1;38;5;220mls /usr/bin | grep ^a | wc -l[0m    [2m# …and count them[0m

Things to notice while you try these:
  - [1;38;5;220m|[0m is Shift+Backslash on most keyboards.
  - Each piece is a normal command; only the connector is new.
  - The pipeline runs left-to-right

; output flows.

[1;38;5;208m4.3 — redirection and globs[0m

A pipe sends output to [1;38;5;244manother program[0m. A redirect sends it
to [1;38;5;244ma file[0m.

  [1;38;5;220m>[0m    write to a file ([1;38;5;196moverwrites[0m if it exists)
  [1;38;5;220m>>[0m   append to a file (creates if missing)
  [1;38;5;220m<[0m    read a file [1;38;5;244minto[0m a command

Examples:
  [1;38;5;220mecho first > greeting.txt[0m        [2m# overwrite[0m
  [1;38;5;220mecho second >> greeting.txt[0m      [2m# append[0m
  [1;38;5;220mcat greeting.txt[0m                 [2m# two lines[0m
  [1;38;5;220mwc -w < poem.txt[0m                 [2m# count words read from poem.txt[0m

Combine with pipes:
  [1;38;5;220mls /usr/bin | sort > programs.txt[0m
  [1;38;5;220mwc -l programs.txt[0m

[1;38;5;244mGlobs[0m match many filenames at once. The shell expands them
[1;38;5;244mbefore[0m the command sees them.

  [1;38;5;220mls *.txt[0m              [2m# every .txt file in this folder[0m

[1;38;5;220mwc -l *.txt[0m           [2m# count lines in each .txt file[0m
  [1;38;5;220mcat *.txt[0m             [2m# print them all back-to-back[0m

[1;38;5;196mPredict before you act.[0m  [1;38;5;220mrm *[0m removes everything
in the current folder. [1;38;5;220mrm *.tmp[0m removes only .tmp files.

[1;38;5;208m▶ Type [1;38;5;220mnext[1;38;5;208m to take Stage 4's gate.[0m

Do these:

[1;38;5;208mSTAGE 5 — Ready for vimtutor[0m

Four lessons, then a gate. By the end, you'll know the difference
between a command that prints-and-exits and one that takes over the
terminal; you'll be able to leave any of them deliberately; and you'll
understand why Vim has [1;38;5;220m:w[0m, [1;38;5;220m:q[0m, and [1;38;5;220m:q![0m.

After the gate, this tutor hands you to [1;38;5;220mvimtutor[0m (if it's
installed on your system) — that is the next step.
